note: One shared glossary. `plain` is the wording the story uses; `term` is the exact technical term shown on hover/tap with `def`. Every factual definition cites quotes that scripts/07_build_glossary.py checks word for word against the source text (a Q&A passage in qa_chunks.json or a committed file). Entries with no factual claim (a unit or a plain re-wording) say so in `kind`.

us_std_atm_1976.citation: U.S. Standard Atmosphere, 1976. NOAA, NASA and U.S. Air Force, NOAA-S/T 76-1562 / NASA-TM-X-74335 (NTRS 19770009539).
us_std_atm_1976.use: Altitude companions for pressures in the story: lower atmosphere (0-11 km) P = 101.325 kPa x (1 + L h / T0)^(-g0 M0 / (R* L)), with T0 = 288.15 K, L = -0.0065 K/m, g0 = 9.80665 m/s2, M0 = 0.0289644 kg/mol, R* = 8.31432 J/(mol K); 11-20 km isothermal at 216.65 K from 22.632 kPa. Height is geopotential (differs from geometric height by < 0.2% below 11 km); shown rounded to 100 m.

atm.def: 1 atm (one standard atmosphere) is defined as 101.325 kPa, Earth's average air pressure at sea level.

bass2.def: BASS-II (Burning and Suppression of Solids - II) burned small acrylic-plastic and fabric samples inside the space station's Microgravity Science Glovebox, varying the airflow and the oxygen.
bass2.plain: BASS-II, a fire experiment on the space station
bass2.src: PSI-25 Comment[Approach]: "Main variables are airflow speed and oxygen concentration" (PSI-25 Burning and Suppression of Solids - II: PSI metadata Comment[Approach]) | BASS-II report p.3: "the atmosphere in the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG)" (BASS-II Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385 (Oct 2021), printed p. 3)

blowoff.def: Blowoff: the flame goes out because the air flowing past it is too fast.
blowoff.plain: the airflow blew the flame out
blowoff.src: BASS-II report p.11: "blowoff extinctions" (BASS-II Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385 (Oct 2021), printed p. 11) | BASS-II report p.66: "consist of a blowoff and new quenching branch" (BASS-II Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385 (Oct 2021), printed p. 66)

bm25.def: BM25 is a standard keyword-ranking formula: passages that share more (and rarer) words with the question rank higher. No AI is involved in this step.

boundary.def: A flammability boundary is the line, in oxygen and airflow, between conditions where a material keeps burning and where its flame goes out.
boundary.plain: the line between burns and doesn't burn
boundary.src: BASS-II report p.94: "O2-flow-velocity flammability boundary" (BASS-II Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385 (Oct 2021), printed p. 94) | BASS-II report p.74: "the flow speed at which the flames extinguished and the last flow speed at which a stable flame was obse" (BASS-II Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385 (Oct 2021), printed p. 74)

cms.def: cm/s: centimetres per second, the speed of the air flowing past the sample (100 cm/s = 1 m/s).

extinction.def: Extinction: the flame goes out. Blowoff (too much airflow) and quenching (too little) are two ways it happens.
extinction.src: BASS-II report p.74: "the flow speed at which the flames extinguished" (BASS-II Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385 (Oct 2021), printed p. 74)

kpa.def: kPa (kilopascal) is a unit of pressure. Earth's air at sea level is 14.7 psi = 101.3 kPa (1 psi = 6.894757 kPa).
kpa.plain: kilopascals, a unit of air pressure
kpa.src: challenge page: "the Earth’s pressure at sea level is 14.7 psi" (docs/ref/challenge_brief.md)

micro.def: Microgravity is the near-weightless free fall of an orbiting spacecraft such as the International Space Station. Without buoyancy, hot gas does not rise, so flames change shape.
micro.plain: near-weightless, like on the space station
micro.src: challenge page: "flames in free fall (i.e., in microgravity) are often dramatically different because of the absence of buoyancy and thus rising hot gases" (docs/ref/challenge_brief.md) | challenge page: "low-gravity combustion experiments, conducted for example on the International Space Station (ISS)" (docs/ref/challenge_brief.md)

moonair.def: Moon-base air: the atmosphere planned for Moon bases and pressurized rovers, 30% or more oxygen at 10.2 psi (70.3 kPa) or less, so astronauts can use spacesuits more easily.
moonair.plain: the air planned for Moon bases
moonair.src: challenge page: "The intermediate oxygen concentration used on the Moon will likely be 30% or greater, with a corresponding pressure of 10.2 psi or less" (docs/ref/challenge_brief.md) | challenge page: "To facilitate spacesuit use, an atmosphere with increased oxygen and reduced pressure compared to Earth’s is expected within the planned Moon Base and pressurized rovers" (docs/ref/challenge_brief.md)

o2fire.def: Moon-base air is planned at 30% oxygen or more, over 40% more than Earth's air, which makes materials much more flammable. NASA prevents fires partly by choosing materials, which depends on knowing their flammability limits.
o2fire.plain: more oxygen makes materials burn more easily
o2fire.src: challenge page: "Compared to Earth’s atmosphere, that’s more than a 40% increase in the oxygen concentration making materials much more flammable" (docs/ref/challenge_brief.md) | challenge page: "Prevention is achieved by controlling ignition sources and through material selection, which depends on understanding flammability limits" (docs/ref/challenge_brief.md)

o2pct.def: O2 % is the share of the gas that is oxygen, by volume (the same as mole %). Earth's normal air is 21% oxygen.
o2pct.plain: share of the air that is oxygen
o2pct.src: PSI-20 Comment[Research Impacts]: "a normal atmosphere of 21% oxygen" (PSI-20 Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator: PSI metadata Comment[Research Impacts]) | NTRS 20160001047 p.3: "is the same as referring to it by its mole percent (21 mole % O2)" (NTRS 20160001047 (O2 partial pressure vs concentration flammability), PDF p. 3)

partial.def: Partial gravity is gravity weaker than Earth's but far above zero, as on the Moon or Mars. PSI holds no fire data from it yet.
partial.src: challenge page: "there is currently no partial-gravity combustion data available in PSI" (docs/ref/challenge_brief.md)

pmma.def: PMMA (polymethylmethacrylate) is acrylic plastic. BASS-II burned it as rods, slabs and thin films.
pmma.src: BASS-II report, abbreviations: "PMMA polymethylmethacrylate (acrylic)" (BASS-II Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385 (Oct 2021), printed p. 2) | BASS-II report p.5: "cast polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) samples were shaped as rods" (BASS-II Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385 (Oct 2021), printed p. 5)

po2.def: Oxygen partial pressure (pO2) is the part of the total pressure that comes from oxygen: O2 fraction x total pressure. Equal pO2 means each breath holds about the same amount of oxygen.
po2.src: NTRS 20160001047: "Oxygen Partial Pressure and Oxygen Concentration Flammability" (NTRS 20160001047 (O2 partial pressure vs concentration flammability), PDF p. 1)

psi.def: PSI (Physical Sciences Informatics, psi.nasa.gov) is NASA's public archive of physical-science experiments, including fire tests on the space station.
psi.src: challenge page: "are being made publicly available through NASA's Physical Science Informatics (PSI) database" (docs/ref/challenge_brief.md)

quench.def: Quenching: at very low airflow the flame becomes too weak to make up for the heat it loses, and goes out.
quench.plain: the flame went out because the airflow was too weak
quench.src: BASS-II report p.66: "quenching branch where the low power flame (due to the reduced temperature) is too weak to compensate for the surface radiative heat loss" (BASS-II Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385 (Oct 2021), printed p. 66)

saffire.def: Saffire (Spacecraft Fire Safety Demonstration) burned large material samples inside Cygnus cargo spacecraft in orbit, to see how a large fire grows in low gravity.
saffire.plain: Saffire, large fire tests in an uncrewed cargo spacecraft
saffire.src: PSI-98 Comment[Objective]: "determine how rapidly a large scale fire grows in low-gravity" (PSI-98 Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I: PSI metadata Comment[Objective]) | Saffire ICES-2024-365 (our summary): "Microgravity (orbiting Cygnus) only" (Flame Frontier Known Limits: Saffire ICES-2024-365)

sibal.def: SIBAL is a fabric of cotton on a fiberglass backing (75% cotton, 25% fiberglass by weight), named after an earlier NASA project, Solid Inflammability Boundary at Low Speeds.
sibal.src: PSI-98 Comment[Approach]: "Sibal consisting of cotton on a fiberglass substrate (75% cotton, 25% fiberglass by weight)" (PSI-98 Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I: PSI metadata Comment[Approach]) | BASS-II report p.94: "The fabric is custom made for a previous project Solid Inflammability Boundary at Low Speeds (SIBAL)" (BASS-II Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385 (Oct 2021), printed p. 94)

solids.def: Solid materials: things like fabric and plastic, as opposed to gas or liquid fuels. NASA's flammability studies for crew cabins focus on them.
solids.plain: solid materials such as fabrics and plastics
solids.src: challenge page: "Flammability studies focus on solid materials such as fabrics and plastics" (docs/ref/challenge_brief.md)

ssce.def: SSCE (Solid Surface Combustion Experiment) was the first combustion experiment flown on the Space Shuttle: flame spread over filter paper and acrylic plastic, over 8 flights.
ssce.plain: SSCE, early fire tests on the Space Shuttle
ssce.src: NTRS 20050177200: "was the first combustion experiment to fly in the space shuttle" (SSCE, NTRS 20050177200 (abstract)) | NTRS 20050177200: "the fuel sample--ashless filter paper" (SSCE, NTRS 20050177200 (abstract)) | NTRS 20050177200: "a polymethyl methacrylate (plexiglass) fuel" (SSCE, NTRS 20050177200 (abstract)) | NTRS 20050177200: "the final two of eight flights" (SSCE, NTRS 20050177200 (abstract))

stretch.def: Stretch rate a (unit 1/s) measures how strongly the oncoming air strains the flame at the sample's tip. It rises with air speed and is larger for thinner rods: a = (3/2)(U/r)(r/r0)^0.5 (BASS-II eq. 6.1).
stretch.plain: how hard the oncoming air strains the flame
stretch.src: BASS-II report p.66: "The flammability map in terms of O2 and stretch rate a" (BASS-II Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385 (Oct 2021), printed p. 66)
